R.q:
Read the passage.

Hospitals are noisier than most people expect. Alarms from monitors and pumps, overhead pages, rolling carts and conversations at nursing stations can push nighttime sound levels well above what sleep researchers recommend for bedrooms.

The noise matters because sleep is part of recovery. Patients who sleep poorly in the hospital often report more pain and more confusion, and they may be slower to regain strength. Staff are affected as well: frequent alarms that turn out to be harmless can lead nurses to respond more slowly to the ones that count.

Some hospitals have tried quiet hours, softer flooring and alarms that alert only the assigned nurse's phone. A few units report better patient sleep scores, although the changes can be costly to install.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Changes such as softer flooring and phone-based alarms are costly for hospitals to install on their units.
Frequent harmless alarms can lead nurses to respond more slowly to the alarms that signal real problems.
Hospitals are noisier than people expect because of monitors, pages, carts and conversations at stations.
Hospital noise disrupts patient sleep and staff response, and some hospitals are testing ways to reduce it.
R.w: Paragraph 1 describes the noise, paragraph 2 explains why it matters for patients and staff, and paragraph 3 describes efforts to reduce it. This option combines all three with the same emphasis as the passage.

n.0: Reversed emphasis: the cost of the changes is a brief qualification at the very end, not the passage's central point.
n.1: Too narrow: alarm fatigue is one detail in the second paragraph.
n.2: Summarizes only the first paragraph and leaves out why the noise matters and what hospitals are doing.

R.q:
Read the leaflet.

Your Child's First Visit to the Dentist
Bring along a favorite toy or blanket so your child has something familiar to hold. At the visit, the hygienist will count your child's teeth with a small mirror; we call it the "tooth parade." At home, avoid words like hurt, shot or drill, which can make a young child anxious before the appointment even begins. Afterward, praise your child for being brave, even if there were a few tears. Before you leave, schedule the next checkup; most children need one every six months. Questions? Call our front desk.

The leaflet is most likely written for which audience?
o: Dental hygienists learning to work with nervous young patients
Young children preparing for their first dental cleaning
Parents of teenagers who feel anxious about dental work
Parents of young children seeing a dentist for the first time
R.w: The leaflet addresses "you" about "your child," tells the reader what to bring, what to say at home and what to schedule, and mentions toys, blankets and a playful "tooth parade." These clues point to parents of young children before a first visit.

n.0: The reader is told what the hygienist will do, so the reader is not the hygienist.
n.1: The child is referred to as "your child," so the reader is the adult, not the child.
n.2: Toys, blankets, a "tooth parade" and a first visit point to young children, not teenagers.

R.q:
Read the paragraph.

(1) Children who go to bed at the same time each night tend to fall asleep faster. (2) A steady bedtime helps set the body's internal clock, which controls when a child begins to feel drowsy. (3) Researchers have linked regular bedtimes to better attention and behavior in school. (4) Teenagers' internal clocks shift later, which is why many feel alert late at night. (5) Even on weekends, keeping bedtime within an hour of the weekday time helps the clock stay steady. (6) Families that build a short routine, such as a bath, a book and lights out, often find that bedtime battles become less frequent.

The main idea of the paragraph is that a consistent bedtime benefits children. Which sentence does NOT support this main idea?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Sentence 5
R.w: Sentence 4 shares a key phrase (internal clock) with the paragraph, but it describes a natural shift in teenagers' clocks, not a benefit of a consistent bedtime for children. The other listed sentences each explain, show or extend that benefit.

n.0: Sentence 3 gives evidence of a benefit: better attention and behavior in school.
n.2: Sentence 2 explains how a steady bedtime helps, by setting the internal clock that controls drowsiness.
n.3: Sentence 5 explains how to keep the benefit on weekends, so it supports the idea of a consistent bedtime.

R.q:
A community health worker is updating a handout on recommended vaccines for adults. She finds two sources that disagree about whether a certain booster is recommended for adults over 65. Source A is a chart from the state health department's website, printed in 2014. Source B is the same department's current online schedule, which notes that its advice was revised last spring after new research was published.

Which source should she rely on, and why?
o: Source B, because online sources are generally more accurate than print
Source B, because it is the current version from the same authority
Source A, because it has been in use longer and has been cited more often
Source A, because a printed chart is more reliable than a web page
R.w: Both sources come from the same authority, so currency decides. Source B reflects the department's latest advice, revised after new research, which matters for health guidance.

n.0: Source B is better because it is current, not because it is online; many online sources are unreliable.
n.2: Age and frequent citation do not outweigh a newer revision from the same authority.
n.3: Format does not decide accuracy; the 2014 chart is simply out of date.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a hospital administrator: Last year we ended fixed visiting hours. Families may now visit at any time, because patients with loved ones nearby report less anxiety and often understand their discharge plans better. To protect rest, we allow two visitors at a time after 9 p.m.

Passage 2
From a nurse's blog: Open visiting has helped many of my patients, and I would not go back. But on night shift, a crowded room can keep a patient awake and slow down care. Hospitals that welcome families should also set quiet hours that visitors respect.

On which point do the two authors agree?
o: Patients recover faster when visitors come during daytime hours.
Nighttime visitors should be limited to two people per patient.
Family presence helps patients, but nighttime visits need some limits.
Open visiting adds to the workload of nurses on the night shift.
R.w: The administrator credits family presence with less anxiety and caps night visitors at two; the nurse says open visiting has helped and calls for quiet hours. Both support families while limiting nights.

n.0: Neither passage compares daytime and nighttime visits for recovery speed.
n.1: The two-visitor rule appears in Passage 1 only; the nurse proposes quiet hours, not a number.
n.3: Slower care at night is the nurse's concern in Passage 2; the administrator does not discuss workload.

R.q:
Passage 1
When I was ten, summer meant leaving the house after breakfast and coming home when the streetlights blinked on. We built forts in the creek bed and settled our arguments ourselves. Those long, unsupervised afternoons taught me how to be a friend.

Passage 2
Every Tuesday night, 12-year-old Amir logs on to a coding club with kids from four states. They debug each other's games, tease each other in the chat, and celebrate birthdays on video. Two of them met in person for the first time this summer and hugged like old friends.

How do the themes of the two passages differ?
o: Passage 1 is about friendship, while Passage 2 is about learning to write code.
Both passages suggest that children today are lonelier than children once were.
Passage 1 rejects technology, while Passage 2 rejects outdoor play for children.
Passage 1 ties friendship to outdoor play; Passage 2 shows it growing through screens.
R.w: Both passages are about how children form friendships. Passage 1 credits unsupervised outdoor play; Passage 2 shows close friendships forming in an online coding club.

n.0: Coding is the setting of Passage 2, but its central idea is friendship, the same subject as Passage 1.
n.1: Passage 2 shows children who are close and connected, so loneliness is not a shared theme.
n.2: This overstates both: Passage 1 never criticizes technology, and Passage 2 never criticizes outdoor play.

R.q:
Read the passage.

For most of the twentieth century, the Harlan textile mill employed nearly half the working adults in Pine Ridge. When the mill closed in 1998, hundreds of families moved away to find work, and the town's population dropped by a third within five years.

With fewer children enrolled, the district merged Pine Ridge's two elementary schools into one. The empty building sat unused until 2015, when a group of residents raised money to turn it into a community health center.

Today the center employs forty people, and its staff includes several former students of the old school.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: Pine Ridge lost a third of its people after the district merged its two elementary schools, which led the mill to close.
Residents of Pine Ridge raised money in 2015 to build a new community health center that now employs forty people.
After the mill closed and families left, Pine Ridge merged its schools, and residents turned the empty one into a clinic.
The Harlan textile mill employed nearly half of Pine Ridge's working adults for most of the twentieth century.
R.w: The passage is a chain of causes and effects: the mill closed, families left, enrollment fell, the schools merged, and residents later turned the empty school into a health center. This option keeps that chain in the correct order.

n.0: Reverses cause and effect: the mill closing caused the population loss, which led to the school merger, not the other way around.
n.1: Distortion: residents converted the old school building rather than building a new center, and the option skips the cause.
n.3: Too narrow: this is background from the first sentence only.

R.q:
Mara checked the supply cart twice before her shift began, then a third time after report. When the charge nurse asked why, Mara pointed to a note taped inside the top drawer. The reminder, written in her own handwriting, dated from the night a missing suction catheter had cost the team four minutes during an emergency. "I'd rather lose thirty seconds now," she said. The charge nurse nodded slowly. The following week, a cart check appeared on the start-of-shift list for every nurse on the unit.

Which conclusion about Mara is best supported by the passage?
o: She does not trust the other nurses on the unit to stock the supply cart correctly.
She was the nurse responsible for the missing catheter on the night of the emergency.
She was asked by the charge nurse to train the other nurses to check their carts.
A past delay she witnessed shapes the way she prepares for each of her shifts.
R.w: The note recalls the night a missing catheter cost four minutes, and Mara says she would rather lose thirty seconds now. Her repeated checks are explained by that earlier delay.

n.0: Nothing in the passage blames other nurses; her checks are tied to one past event, not to distrust of coworkers.
n.1: The note is in her handwriting, but the passage never says who left the catheter out; this is an assumption.
n.2: The charge nurse added a cart check to the shift list; the passage never says Mara was asked to train anyone.

R.q:
Passage 1
Protect yourself while you are here. Clean your hands before you eat, after you use the bathroom, and when you enter or leave a patient's room. Rub hand sanitizer over all surfaces of your hands until they are dry, about 20 seconds. It is okay to ask your care team, "Did you clean your hands?"

Passage 2
To: All clinical staff. Hand hygiene audits on Units 4 and 5 found compliance of 71 percent in March, below our goal of 90 percent. Beginning May 1, unit managers will post monthly audit results, and units below goal will complete a refresher module.

Which statement best describes a difference between the passages?
o: Passage 1 is written for patients and visitors; Passage 2, for hospital staff.
Passage 1 gives infection data; Passage 2 gives steps for cleaning hands.
Passage 1 is written for newly hired nurses; Passage 2, for the hospital's unit managers.
Passage 1 gives directions in the second person; Passage 2 tells a nurse's personal story.
R.w: Passage 1 speaks to "you" while you are here and invites you to ask your care team, so its audience is patients and visitors. Passage 2 is a memo addressed to all clinical staff about audit results.

n.1: This reverses the passages: Passage 1 gives the steps, and Passage 2 gives audit data.
n.2: Passage 1 invites readers to ask their care team, so it addresses patients and visitors; Passage 2 goes to all clinical staff, not just managers.
n.3: Passage 1 does address "you," but Passage 2 is a memo reporting audit data and a new policy, not a personal story.

R.q:
Our beagle, Biscuit, has never once come when called. But on Thanksgiving, as my uncle set the turkey on the counter and turned to find the carving knife, Biscuit materialized like a furry magician. By the time my uncle turned back, the turkey was gone, and so was the dog. We found them both under my parents' bed twenty minutes later: Biscuit asleep with his paws around a drumstick, looking prouder than any dog has a right to look. We had pizza for dinner. Biscuit had nothing to eat for the rest of the day, and he did not seem to mind.

What is the author's primary purpose in this passage?
o: to explain how to prepare a holiday meal for a large family
to entertain readers with a funny story about a family dog
to persuade readers to keep food out of a dog's reach
to inform readers about why beagles are hard to train
R.w: The passage tells a story with comic details (the "furry magician," the proud dog hugging a drumstick, pizza for Thanksgiving dinner) and makes no argument or lesson. Its purpose is to entertain.

n.0: The holiday meal is the setting of the story, not a set of instructions.
n.2: A reader might draw this lesson, but the author never urges it; the story is told for amusement.
n.3: The author mentions that Biscuit never comes when called, but offers no information about beagles as a breed or about training.

R.q:
Read the description of the pie chart.

Title: How Surveyed Nursing Students Commute to Campus
Total surveyed: 400 students
Sections:
Drive alone: 45%
Public transit: 25%
Carpool: 15%
Walk or bike: 10%
Other: 5%
Note: Students who use more than one method were asked to choose the one they use most often. The survey was emailed to all first- and second-year students in September, and 400 of them completed it.

According to the chart, how many of the surveyed students carpool to campus?
o: 40 students
15 students
100 students
60 students
R.w: The chart shows percentages of 400 students. Carpool is 15%, and 15% of 400 is 0.15 x 400 = 60 students.

n.0: 40 students is the walk-or-bike group (10% of 400).
n.1: Treats the percentage (15%) as a count of students.
n.2: 100 students is the public transit group (25% of 400).

R.q:
Read the description of the floor plan.

First Floor, Wellness Center
The main entrance is in the south wall and opens into the lobby. The reception desk stands against the north wall of the lobby, facing the entrance. From the east side of the lobby, a hallway runs north. Along the hallway's east side are Exam Room 1, Exam Room 2 and Exam Room 3, in that order from south to north. On the hallway's west side, directly across from Exam Room 2, is the lab. The restrooms are at the far north end of the hallway. West of the lobby is the pharmacy, which has its own outside door in the west wall.

Based on the floor plan, which room is closest to the restrooms?
o: Exam Room 3
Exam Room 1
The pharmacy
The lab
R.w: The restrooms are at the north end of the hallway. Exam Room 3 is the farthest north of the rooms along the hallway, so it is closest.

n.1: Exam Room 1 is the farthest south along the hallway, nearest the lobby.
n.2: The pharmacy is west of the lobby, on the opposite side of the building from the hallway.
n.3: The lab sits across from Exam Room 2, in the middle of the hallway, south of Exam Room 3.

R.q:
How to use your inhaler
This medicine works best when it reaches deep into your lungs. Breathe out fully, seal your lips around the mouthpiece, and press the canister as you begin a slow, deep breath. Then hold your breath for 10 seconds. If you breathe in quickly, much of the medicine lands on the back of your throat instead of reaching your lungs, and over time you may notice a hoarse voice. Rinse your mouth with water after each use to remove any medicine left in your mouth.

Devon presses the canister and then takes a quick, sharp breath each time he uses his inhaler. Based on the leaflet, what is most likely to happen?
o: Less of the medicine will reach his lungs, and his voice may become hoarse.
The medicine will reach his lungs faster and so begin to work sooner.
He will need to hold his breath longer than 10 seconds to make up for it.
Rinsing his mouth will carry the medicine from his throat to his lungs.
R.w: The leaflet says a quick breath leaves much of the medicine on the back of the throat instead of in the lungs and may cause a hoarse voice over time.

n.1: This reverses the leaflet: a quick breath sends less medicine to the lungs, not more.
n.2: The leaflet offers no longer breath-hold as a fix; the fix it implies is a slow, deep breath.
n.3: The leaflet says rinsing removes medicine left in the mouth; it does not move medicine to the lungs.

R.q:
When my grandmother broke her hip, the nearest rehabilitation center was two hours away, and our family could visit only on Sundays. Rural counties like ours need small rehab units attached to local hospitals. Patients recover better when family members can visit often, according to a review of 22 studies on stroke and hip-fracture recovery. Some health officials argue that small units cannot afford specialized staff. But traveling therapists already rotate among rural hospitals in neighboring counties, and the state could fund the same model here. Write to your state representative this week.

Which statement best describes how the argument is organized?
o: A story introduces a claim, which is supported, challenged, and then defended.
A claim is stated, and the author changes position after weighing an objection.
A problem is described in detail, and the author declines to propose a remedy.
Two opposing views receive equal weight, and readers are left to decide.
R.w: The grandmother's story leads to the claim (rural rehab units), followed by evidence (the 22-study review), an objection (staffing costs), a rebuttal (traveling therapists), and a call to action.

n.1: The author answers the objection with traveling therapists and keeps the original position.
n.2: The author proposes rehab units and a state-funded therapist model.
n.3: The author clearly takes one side and urges readers to act on it.

R.q: Read the passage. Select the sentence that most clearly reveals the author's own perspective on the law.

parts.t: A new state law that takes effect in January requires nurses to complete 30 hours of continuing education every two years to renew their licenses.
Supporters of the law say the requirement will keep patient care up to date.
Hospital administrators, by contrast, warn that it will make staffing shortages worse.
A survey by the state nursing association found that 60 percent of its members already complete more than 30 hours.
Both groups raise fair points, but the sponsors' failure to explain who will pay for the courses is hard to excuse.

sn.c: A new state law that takes effect in January requires nurses to complete 30 hours of continuing education every two years to renew their licenses.
sn.a: Supporters of the law say the requirement will keep patient care up to date.
sn.b: Hospital administrators, by contrast, warn that it will make staffing shortages worse.
sn.e: A survey by the state nursing association found that 60 percent of its members already complete more than 30 hours.
sn.d: Both groups raise fair points, but the sponsors' failure to explain who will pay for the courses is hard to excuse.

R.w: Sentence 5 is the only place the author speaks in the author's own voice. "Fair points" and "hard to excuse" are the author's judgments of the debate and of the law's sponsors.

n.a: This reports what supporters say. The author is describing a view held by others, not taking a position.
n.b: This reports the administrators' warning. Attributing it to them shows it is their view, not necessarily the author's.
n.c: The start date and the 30-hour rule are checkable facts about the law and carry no judgment.
n.e: This reports survey data. The author does not say what the result means or whether it matters.

R.q:
A school district surveyed 1,200 high school students about sleep. Students who used their phones in bed after 10 p.m. reported sleeping about 50 minutes less on school nights than students who did not, even though both groups reported going to bed at similar times. The district then launched a campaign urging families to charge phones outside the bedroom. Early results from 80 families who joined a trial of the campaign show that the students fell asleep about 20 minutes sooner on average.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Students who use phones in bed go to bed later than students who do not use them.
Students who join the campaign can expect to gain about 50 minutes of sleep on school nights.
Phone use in bed may delay sleep even when students go to bed at the same time as their peers.
Most high school students in the district probably use their phones in bed after 10 p.m.
R.w: Both groups went to bed at similar times, yet phone users slept about 50 minutes less, and removing phones helped trial students fall asleep sooner. Together these details support the idea that phone use delays falling asleep.

n.0: This contradicts the passage, which says both groups reported going to bed at similar times.
n.1: This over-extends the data: 50 minutes was the survey gap, but the trial showed students falling asleep about 20 minutes sooner.
n.3: The passage gives no share of students who use phones in bed, so a majority cannot be concluded.

R.q:
Gabriela Ruiz is drafting a letter to her city council about drinking water. Her first draft begins, "The city's tap water is unsafe to drink." Her teacher points out that this sentence is an opinion as written. She suggests that Gabriela open with a fact that council members could verify for themselves, and then state her own view in a later sentence, so that her argument rests on evidence rather than on feeling.

Which revision follows her teacher's advice?
o: Experts agree that the city's tap water is probably unsafe for young children.
In a 2023 city test, water from 12 homes had lead above the federal action level.
The city's tap water is far too risky for families with babies and young children.
The city's tap water tastes worse than the bottled water sold in local stores.
R.w: A dated test with a stated number of homes and a federal standard can be checked against the city's test records, so it is a verifiable fact.

n.0: "Probably" signals a judgment, and claiming that experts agree does not make a judgment a fact. Expert opinion is still opinion.
n.2: "Far too risky" is a judgment about how much risk is acceptable, so the revision is still an opinion.
n.3: Taste is a matter of personal judgment; "tastes worse" cannot be proven.

R.q:
When Jasmine opened the supply closet at the start of her shift, she found it in disarray. Rolls of gauze, boxes of gloves and packets of syringes were jumbled together on the same shelves, and nothing was where the labels said it would be. Every item on her restocking checklist was there, but it took her twenty minutes to sort everything back into place.

As used in the passage, the word disarray most nearly means
o: a shortage of supplies.
a state of disrepair.
a state of disorder.
an unsanitary condition.
R.w: "Jumbled together," "nothing was where the labels said" and the need to "sort everything back into place" all describe a mess. Disarray means disorder.

n.0: Every item on her checklist was there; the problem was where the supplies were, not how many there were.
n.1: "Disrepair" looks similar, but it means broken or damaged. Nothing in the closet is described as broken, and Jasmine fixes the problem by sorting, not repairing.
n.3: Nothing mentions dirt or contamination; the items are mixed up, not unclean.

R.q:
Monday mornings in the hospital admissions office are organized chaos. The phones ring nonstop, and the line at the front desk stretches like a ribbon to the main doors. Clerks wade through a sea of paperwork while the old printer in the corner coughs out one form after another. Somehow, every patient is registered by noon.

Which phrase from the passage is an oxymoron?
o: organized chaos
a sea of paperwork
stretches like a ribbon
coughs out one form
R.w: An oxymoron joins two words with opposite meanings. "Organized" and "chaos" contradict each other, and together they capture an office that is busy and messy yet still gets the job done.

n.1: This is a metaphor: it calls a large amount of paperwork a sea without using "like" or "as."
n.2: This is a simile: it compares the line to a ribbon using "like."
n.3: This is personification: coughing is a human action given to a printer.

R.q:
Read the news brief.

The Fairmont City Council approved a new bike-share program on Tuesday, two weeks after a public hearing at which more than sixty residents spoke. The hearing itself had been scheduled after a petition with 4,000 signatures reached the mayor's office in March. Under the plan, bikes will appear at 40 stations by June, following a month-long test with city employees in May. Riders will pay $1 to unlock a bike and 15 cents per minute.

According to the news brief, which of these events happened first?
o: The city council approved the bike-share program.
A petition with 4,000 signatures reached the mayor.
More than sixty residents spoke at a public hearing.
City employees began testing the bikes in May.
R.w: The hearing was scheduled after the petition arrived in March, and the council vote came two weeks after the hearing. The employee test is planned for later. So the petition came first, even though it is mentioned after the vote.

n.0: Order of mention trap: the vote is mentioned first but came two weeks after the hearing.
n.2: The hearing was scheduled after the petition reached the mayor.
n.3: The May test is a future step, after the council's approval.

R.q:
Each winter, clinic phones ring with requests for antibiotics to treat colds. Many callers believe the drugs will help them get over a cold sooner. Colds, however, are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses. Taking antibiotics when they are not needed can cause side effects such as diarrhea and rashes, and it helps bacteria become resistant to the drugs. Rest, fluids and time remain the main treatment for most colds.

Which misconception does the passage seek to correct?
o: That antibiotics will help a person recover from a cold faster
That colds are caused by viruses rather than by bacteria
That antibiotics can cause side effects such as diarrhea and rashes
That rest and fluids are the main treatment for most colds
R.w: The passage reports the belief that antibiotics shorten a cold and then explains why it is wrong: antibiotics act on bacteria, and colds are viral. A commonly held but incorrect belief is a misconception.

n.1: This is the correct information the author uses to correct the misconception, not the misconception itself.
n.2: The author states this as a fact to show why unneeded antibiotics are harmful.
n.3: The author endorses this as the accurate treatment advice; it is not presented as a mistaken belief.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Five blocks sit in a row. From left to right they are red, blue, green, yellow and white. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the arrangement left by the step before it.
1. Swap the second and fourth blocks.
2. Move the block at the far left to the far right.
3. Place a black block between the green block and the blue block.
4. Remove the block that is second from the right.

What is the final order of the blocks, from left to right?
o: yellow, black, blue, white, red
white, red, yellow, green, blue
yellow, green, black, blue, white
yellow, green, black, blue, red
R.w: Step 1: red, yellow, green, blue, white. Step 2: yellow, green, blue, white, red. Step 3: yellow, green, black, blue, white, red. Step 4 removes the second block from the right (white): yellow, green, black, blue, red.

n.0: Removes the block second from the left (green) instead of second from the right.
n.1: Step 2 was reversed: the far-right block was moved to the far left.
n.2: Removes the block at the far right (red) instead of the one second from the right.

R.q: Kayla takes this medicine in the evening, as her doctor advised. At 9 p.m. she realizes she has not taken tonight's tablet. Select the sentence from the leaflet that tells her what to do.

parts.t: Take one tablet each morning with a full glass of water.
If you miss a morning dose, take it as soon as you remember that same day.
If you do not remember until the next morning, skip the missed tablet and take only your usual dose.
Do not take two tablets at once to make up for a missed dose.
If your doctor has told you to take this medicine in the evening, you may take a missed evening dose up until bedtime that night.
Store the tablets at room temperature, away from moisture.

sn.a: Take one tablet each morning with a full glass of water.
sn.b: If you miss a morning dose, take it as soon as you remember that same day.
sn.c: If you do not remember until the next morning, skip the missed tablet and take only your usual dose.
sn.d: Do not take two tablets at once to make up for a missed dose.
sn.e: If your doctor has told you to take this medicine in the evening, you may take a missed evening dose up until bedtime that night.
sn.f: Store the tablets at room temperature, away from moisture.

R.w: Kayla is an evening user who remembers before bedtime on the same night. Sentence 5 covers exactly that case: a missed evening dose may be taken up until bedtime that night.

n.a: This gives the usual morning timing. It does not address a missed dose or an evening schedule.
n.b: This rule covers a missed morning dose, but Kayla takes her tablet in the evening.
n.c: This applies when the dose is not remembered until the next morning. Kayla remembered the same night.
n.d: This warns against doubling up, which Kayla is not planning to do. It does not tell her what to do with tonight's tablet.
n.f: Storage instructions do not address missed doses.

R.q:
Welcome to the Oakridge Family Clinic. As you enter through the main doors, the check-in desk is directly in front of you. The waiting area lies to your right, with a children's play corner along its far wall. To the left of the check-in desk, a short hallway leads to exam rooms 1 through 6. The lab is at the end of that hallway, across from the restrooms. The pharmacy window is just outside the main doors, to the left of the entrance.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
order of importance
spatial order
classification
R.w: The passage locates each area by its position relative to the visitor ("directly in front of you," "to your right," "at the end of that hallway"). Organizing details by location is spatial order.

n.0: "As you enter" sets a starting point, but the passage maps where things are rather than narrating events in time.
n.1: No area is ranked as more or less important; each is placed by location.
n.3: The areas are not sorted into types or categories; they are positioned on a mental map.

R.q:
Read the glossary from a patient guide.

Glossary
Benign: not cancerous; does not spread to other parts of the body.
Biopsy: removal of a small sample of tissue to be examined under a microscope.
Malignant: cancerous; able to invade nearby tissue and spread.
Metastasis: the spread of cancer from the place where it started to another part of the body.
Oncologist: a doctor who specializes in treating cancer.
Remission: a decrease in or disappearance of the signs of cancer.

A patient's report reads, "The biopsy showed a benign growth." Based on the glossary, what does this sentence mean?
o: Signs of cancer in the growth have decreased since the last exam.
A doctor who treats cancer found a growth that needs a closer look.
A tissue sample showed cancer that has spread to another part of the body.
A tissue sample showed a growth that is not cancerous.
R.w: A biopsy is a tissue sample examined under a microscope, and benign means not cancerous. Together: the sample showed a growth that is not cancer.

n.0: This describes remission, a different glossary term.
n.1: This confuses biopsy with oncologist; a biopsy is a tissue sample, not a doctor.
n.2: This combines malignant and metastasis, the terms that describe cancer that spreads.

R.q:
For a research methods class, Sofia reads an article in a peer-reviewed nursing journal. In it, the authors describe a study they conducted at three hospitals, comparing two methods of preventing pressure injuries in 400 patients. The article explains their methods, presents their data in tables, and discusses what their results mean. Sofia lists the article as a secondary source because it was published in a journal and includes the authors' analysis.

Is Sofia's classification correct?
o: No; it is a primary source because the authors report their own original study.
Yes; it is a secondary source because it appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.
Yes; it is a secondary source because it interprets data using statistics.
No; it is a tertiary source because journals are indexed in library databases.
R.w: A research article in which the authors present their own study and data is a primary source. Analysis of one's own results does not make it secondary; a review of other people's studies would be.

n.1: Publication in a journal does not decide the type; journals publish both primary studies and secondary reviews.
n.2: Researchers analyzing their own data are still reporting original work, so the article stays primary.
n.3: Being indexed in a database does not make an article tertiary; indexes are tertiary, the articles they list are not.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The Ruiz Family Clinic opened in a converted storefront in 1994 with one doctor and two nurses. In 2001 it moved to a former bank building on Fourth Street, which gave it room for a small pharmacy. A dental wing followed in 2008, paid for by a state grant the clinic had first applied for in 2005. When the clinic celebrated its twenty-fifth anniversary in 2019, it employed 64 people, and plans were under way for a behavioral health center, which opened in 2022.

According to the passage, in what year did the clinic first have room for a pharmacy?
R.w: The passage says that the 2001 move to the former bank building gave the clinic room for a small pharmacy.

n.0: 1994 is when the clinic opened in a storefront; no pharmacy is mentioned then.
n.2: 2005 is when the clinic first applied for the grant that later paid for the dental wing.
n.3: 2008 is when the dental wing was added.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Directions to the Westside Health Fair
From the Main Street bus stop, walk two blocks north to Elm Avenue and turn left. If the community center's front entrance is closed, go around to the side door on Birch Lane; otherwise, enter through the front. Once inside, check in at the welcome table. Visitors who preregistered online pick up a name badge; all other visitors fill out a paper form first. Free blood pressure checks are in Room 104, to the right of the welcome table, and flu shots are in Room 110, at the end of the hall.

Gloria did not preregister. When she arrives, the front entrance is open.

According to the directions, what should Gloria do immediately after entering?
o: Pick up her name badge at the welcome table
Go straight to Room 104 for a blood pressure check
Walk around to the side door on Birch Lane
Check in at the welcome table and fill out a paper form
R.w: The front entrance is open, so Gloria enters there. The next step for every visitor is to check in at the welcome table, and because she did not preregister, she fills out a paper form.

n.0: Badges are for visitors who preregistered online, and Gloria did not.
n.1: Skips the check-in step that every visitor completes first.
n.2: The side door is used when the front entrance is closed; Gloria found it open.

R.q:
Read the description of the line graph.

Title: Average Daily Steps of Walking Club Members, Weeks 1 to 6
Vertical axis: Average steps per day
Horizontal axis: Week of the program
Plotted points:
Week 1: 4,200
Week 2: 5,100
Week 3: 5,900
Week 4: 6,400
Week 5: 6,500
Week 6: 6,550
The points are joined by a single line. The club meets three times a week at a city park.

Which statement is best supported by the graph?
o: Average steps rose quickly in the early weeks and then leveled off.
Average steps rose by about the same amount each week of the program.
Members will be averaging more than 8,000 steps a day by week 10.
Members walked fewer steps per day in week 6 than they did in week 4.
R.w: The weekly gains were 900, 800, 500, 100 and 50 steps. Large early increases followed by very small ones mean the line climbs steeply and then flattens.

n.1: The gains shrank from 900 steps to 50 steps, so they were not equal.
n.2: Extrapolates beyond the graph, and the shrinking gains suggest the trend is leveling off, not continuing upward.
n.3: Week 6 (6,550) is higher than week 4 (6,400).

R.q:
The hospital spent $2 million on new records software last year, and nurses were promised faster access to patient information. Instead, finding a single lab result now takes six clicks and two passwords, and the system logs users out after five minutes. For the nurses on the night shift, the new software has become a locked door between them and their patients.

In the final sentence, the author's description of the software as "a locked door" suggests that the software
o: keeps patient records more secure than before.
is closed to nurses who work the night shift.
blocks nurses from the information they need.
physically separates the nurses' station from rooms.
R.w: The details before the metaphor (six clicks, two passwords, frequent logouts) show nurses struggling to reach patient information. The "locked door" stands for that barrier.

n.0: Locks can suggest security, but the passage criticizes the software for slowing nurses down; it never praises its protection of records.
n.1: Night-shift nurses are mentioned as the group most affected, but they can still use the system; the passage describes difficulty, not a ban.
n.3: This reads the metaphor literally; the software is not a physical barrier between rooms.

R.q:
Read the instructions.

Home Blood Pressure Log: Instructions from Dr. Kim's Office
Sit quietly for 5 minutes before measuring, with your feet flat and your arm resting at heart level. Take two readings, one minute apart, and record both.
If either top number is 180 or higher, wait 5 minutes and measure again. If it is still 180 or higher, call 911 if you have chest pain, shortness of breath or trouble speaking; otherwise, call our office right away.
If both top numbers are between 140 and 179, record them and bring the log to your next visit.
If both top numbers are below 140, record them as usual.

Mr. Adeyemi's two readings have top numbers of 184 and 176. Five minutes later, his top number is 182. He has no chest pain, shortness of breath or trouble speaking.

According to the instructions, what should Mr. Adeyemi do?
o: Call Dr. Kim's office right away
Wait another 5 minutes and take two more readings
Record the readings and bring the log to his next visit
Call 911, because one of his readings was 180 or higher
R.w: One first reading (184) was 180 or higher, so he re-measured after 5 minutes. The repeat (182) was still 180 or higher. He has none of the listed symptoms, so the "otherwise" branch applies: call the office right away.

n.1: He has already waited and re-measured once, as directed; the instructions do not call for a further wait.
n.2: This applies when both readings are between 140 and 179; his were 184 and 176, and the repeat was 182.
n.3: Calling 911 applies only with chest pain, shortness of breath or trouble speaking, and he has none of these.

R.q:
Read the passage.

By the third week of flu season, the clinic's waiting room had become a tide that never went out. Patients filled every chair by eight in the morning, and by noon a line stretched past the pharmacy window. The receptionists stopped looking up from their screens. Dr. Patel ate lunch standing in the supply closet, and the nurses traded their usual jokes for quick nods. Still, every patient who came through the door was seen before the clinic closed, even when that meant locking up after nine at night.

The phrase "a tide that never went out" suggests that the waiting room
o: stayed full as new patients kept arriving throughout the day
emptied each afternoon after the busy morning rush ended
was busiest during the hours after the clinic had closed
was flooded during a storm that delayed patients' visits
R.w: A tide that never goes out stays high. The details that follow (chairs full by eight, a line by noon, staff working past nine) confirm the room stayed crowded as patients kept coming all day.

n.1: Opposite of the metaphor: the tide never went out, and the line grew by noon.
n.2: Misreads the detail about locking up late, which shows staff stayed to finish, not that the room was busiest after closing.
n.3: Takes the metaphor literally; nothing in the passage describes water or a storm.

R.q:
Carlos is writing a paper on his state's rules about how many hours a week 16-year-olds may work during the school year. He knows the legislature changed the rules two years ago. He has found a 2015 newspaper article on teen work hours, a blog post by a law firm that advertises its employment services, an encyclopedia article on child labor laws in the United States, and the state labor department's website.

Which source should Carlos use to state the current rule accurately?
o: The law firm's blog post, because lawyers write it for readers with legal questions
The encyclopedia article, because it summarizes child labor laws in every state
The state labor department's website, because it posts the state's current rules
The 2015 newspaper article, because it reports on teen work hours in his state
R.w: The state agency that enforces the rules publishes them officially, and its website reflects the change made two years ago. It is the most authoritative and current source.

n.0: A law firm's promotional blog may be accurate, but it is not the official source and has a business purpose.
n.1: A general encyclopedia article on national laws is less specific and may not reflect his state's recent change.
n.3: An article from 2015 predates the change two years ago, so it may describe the old rule.

R.q:
(1) The Eastside branch library should stay open until 9 p.m. on weeknights instead of closing at 6. (2) Many adults in our neighborhood work until 5:30 and cannot reach the branch before it closes. (3) When the branch tested evening hours last fall, it checked out 1,800 more items in two months. (4) Some board members say the extra hours would cost too much in staff pay. (5) However, the test was staffed by volunteers from the Friends of the Library, who have offered to continue. (6) Our neighbors deserve a library they can actually use.

Which sentence is a rebuttal?
o: Sentence 5
Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
R.w: Sentence 4 raises an objection (staff costs). Sentence 5, beginning with "However," answers that objection by noting volunteers covered the test and have offered to continue. A rebuttal is a response to a counterclaim.

n.1: Sentence 3 is evidence from the trial period supporting the claim.
n.2: Sentence 2 is a reason supporting the claim; it does not answer an objection.
n.3: Sentence 4 is the counterclaim itself, the objection that Sentence 5 rebuts.

R.q:
Companies should encourage walking meetings for small-group brainstorming. Many offices book every conference room by 9 a.m., and walking meetings need no reserved space. In a university study, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative uses for everyday objects while walking than while sitting. Walking also burns more calories than sitting at a conference table, which may matter to employees who spend most of the day at a desk. "I like getting fresh air in the middle of the day," said one employee at a firm that tried the idea.

Which sentence from the passage best supports the author's main claim?
o: In a university study, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative uses for everyday objects while walking.
"I like getting fresh air in the middle of the day," said one employee at a firm that tried the idea.
Many offices book every conference room by 9 a.m., and walking meetings need no reserved space.
Walking also burns more calories than sitting at a conference table, which may matter to employees who spend most of the day at a desk.
R.w: Step 1: the main claim is about brainstorming, a creative task. Step 2: the study showing about 60 percent more creative ideas while walking supports that specific claim most directly.

n.1: One employee's preference is a weak anecdote and concerns fresh air, not idea generation.
n.2: Room shortages explain a convenience, not why walking meetings improve brainstorming.
n.3: Calories relate to health, a side benefit rather than the brainstorming claim.

R.q:
Amara is preparing a presentation on childhood asthma rates in her state. Her teacher wants students to include one example of each type of source in their bibliographies. Amara has already found a primary source and a secondary source and needs a tertiary source. She has four other items on her desk, gathered from the school library and an online research database.

Which item is a tertiary source?
o: A medical encyclopedia entry that briefly summarizes what asthma is
A review article that compares the results of several asthma studies
A journal article reporting the results of the authors' own survey of parents
A recorded interview in which a researcher describes her asthma study
R.w: Encyclopedias are tertiary sources: they compile and condense information from primary and secondary sources into brief reference entries.

n.1: A review article analyzes and summarizes other researchers' studies, which makes it a secondary source.
n.2: An article reporting the authors' own survey is original research, a primary source.
n.3: A researcher describing her own study firsthand is a primary source.

R.q:
The city plans to build a five-story parking garage on the empty lot at Elm and Third Streets. The project would add 420 spaces and cost $11 million, paid for by a bond measure on the November ballot. City planners call the garage "badly needed" and say it would serve visitors to the hospital, the library and the new courthouse. Voters should see this money pit for what it is: a gift to downtown developers at the expense of ordinary taxpayers. Construction would take about 18 months.

Which phrase from the passage most clearly reveals the author's bias?
o: call the garage "badly needed"
paid for by a bond measure
this money pit
the empty lot at Elm and Third Streets
R.w: "Money pit" is loaded language: a negative label that pushes readers to see the garage as wasteful before any evidence is weighed. That emotional slant reveals the author's bias against the project.

n.0: "Badly needed" is a judgment, but it belongs to the city planners, whom the author quotes. Reporting another group's view is not the author's own slant, and the planners' view is the opposite of the author's.
n.1: This states how the project would be financed, a neutral and checkable detail.
n.3: "Empty lot" describes the site's current condition and can be checked; it carries no judgment.

R.q:
Many older adults in Lakeview County miss medical appointments because they no longer drive and the nearest bus stop is more than a mile from the clinic. To fix this, the county launched a ride program last spring. First, a patient calls the clinic at least two days before the visit. Next, a dispatcher schedules a volunteer driver. Then the driver picks the patient up at home and waits during the appointment. In its first six months, the program provided 1,800 rides, and missed appointments fell by a third.

Which of the following best describes the overall organization of the passage?
o: cause and effect, because it explains why patients miss visits
compare and contrast, because it gives results before and after
chronological order, because it lists the steps a patient follows
problem and solution, because it presents a need and a response
R.w: The passage opens with a problem (missed appointments due to lack of transportation), describes the county's ride program as the fix, and reports its results. The ordered steps and the opening cause are parts of that larger problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: "Because" explains the problem in the first sentence, but most of the passage describes the program created to solve it.
n.1: A drop in missed appointments shows the solution worked; the passage does not set two subjects side by side.
n.2: "First," "next" and "then" order the steps of the solution, but they cover one section, not the passage as a whole.

R.q:
Since the new staffing rules took effect, each nurse on our unit has cared for no more than five patients per shift, down from seven. I finally have time to explain a new medication properly, to notice when a patient's breathing changes, and to eat lunch sitting down. Management keeps talking about the cost of hiring more staff. They are not the ones running between rooms at 3 a.m. when two call lights go off at once.

The author of the passage is most likely
o: a reporter writing a news story about staffing rules.
a hospital administrator reviewing the cost of new staff.
a patient who was recently treated on the unit.
a nurse who works shifts on the unit.
R.w: The author refers to "our unit," describes caring for patients and explaining medications, and contrasts the writer's own night-shift experience with management's view. These details point to a staff nurse's perspective.

n.0: A news reporter would write in a neutral voice, but this author writes from personal, first-hand experience.
n.1: The author criticizes management for focusing on cost, which is the opposite of an administrator's perspective.
n.2: The author describes caring for several patients at once, which a patient would not do.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Rosa had worked at the corner bakery for three years by the time she enrolled in night classes at the community college. She kept her weekday job until she finished her prerequisites, then switched to weekend shifts when her clinical rotations began. Those two years were the hardest of her life. She passed her licensing exam the summer after graduation and started at County General that fall, but she still stops by the bakery every Saturday for a cinnamon roll.

According to the passage, which event happened immediately after Rosa finished her prerequisites?
o: She passed her nursing licensing exam.
She started working at County General.
She enrolled in night classes at the college.
She switched to weekend shifts at the bakery.
R.w: Rosa kept her weekday job "until she finished her prerequisites, then switched to weekend shifts" when clinical rotations began. The signal word "then" marks the next event.

n.0: The licensing exam came the summer after graduation, well after the switch to weekends.
n.1: She started at County General in the fall after passing her exam, the last event.
n.2: She enrolled in night classes before taking her prerequisites.

R.q:
Passage 1
From the school nurse: Students who eat breakfast tend to pay closer attention during morning classes. But not every breakfast helps equally. A meal with protein and whole grains, such as eggs and toast, keeps energy steady until lunch, while a frosted pastry often leads to a slump by mid-morning.

Passage 2
From a nutrition column: Studies on breakfast and body weight have produced mixed results, and skipping breakfast does not appear to cause weight gain by itself. What people eat over the whole day matters more. A sugary muffin at 7 a.m. is no better a choice than waiting until a balanced lunch.

Which idea is expressed in both passages?
o: The kind of food eaten matters, not simply whether a meal is eaten.
Eating breakfast improves students' attention during morning classes.
Skipping breakfast has little effect on a person's body weight.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day for good health.
R.w: Passage 1 contrasts eggs and toast with a frosted pastry; Passage 2 says a sugary muffin is no better than waiting for a balanced lunch. Both stress food quality over the fact of eating.

n.1: This is the central claim of Passage 1 only; Passage 2 does not discuss attention.
n.2: This comes from Passage 2 only; Passage 1 does not discuss weight.
n.3: Neither passage says this; Passage 2 suggests breakfast is not essential for weight.

R.q:
Read the memo.

To: All Third-Floor Staff
From: Janet Liu, Nurse Manager
Date: March 3
Subject: Supply room

Starting Monday, the third-floor supply room will be locked at all times, and staff will badge in to enter. Each item removed must be scanned at the new station by the door. Please do not prop the door open, even during busy shifts. Last month's inventory showed that we were billed for far more wound-care supplies than were charted for patients. Thank you for helping us keep costs under control.

Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the memo?
o: The manager believes supplies have been leaving the room without being recorded.
The supply room was previously locked during night shifts but not day shifts.
The hospital plans to stop stocking wound-care supplies on the third floor.
Staff members have been taking wound-care supplies home for their own use.
R.w: The memo pairs new controls (locking, badging, scanning each item) with a gap between supplies billed and supplies charted. The most reasonable inference is that the manager thinks items are being removed without a record.

n.1: Unsupported: the memo says nothing about the room's earlier locking schedule.
n.2: Unsupported: the memo changes how supplies are accessed, not whether they are stocked.
n.3: Overreaches: unrecorded use could come from charting errors or waste; the memo never accuses anyone of taking supplies home.

R.q:
Puzzle Port, a smartphone game, launched in March. The table shows weekly downloads.
Week | Event | Downloads
March 1 | Launch | 9,000
March 15 | none | 4,100
April 12 | Update with new levels | 8,600
April 26 | none | 4,300
May 24 | Update with new levels | 8,900
June 7 | none | 4,200
The company has announced its next update with new levels for the week of July 5, with no other changes planned.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage and table?
o: Downloads will drop after July 5 because players dislike frequent updates.
Downloads will peak in the weeks before July 5 as players hear about the update.
Downloads will spike in the week of July 5 and fall back within about two weeks.
Downloads will rise each week through the rest of the summer after July 5.
R.w: Each launch or update produced a jump to roughly 8,600 to 9,000 downloads that fell back to about 4,000 within two weeks. The next update should follow the same pattern.

n.0: Downloads rose after every earlier update; nothing in the table suggests players dislike updates.
n.1: In the table, downloads rose in the update weeks themselves, not before them.
n.3: Earlier spikes faded within two weeks rather than building, so steady growth reverses the established pattern.

R.q:
Last year, the Oakmont Public Library stopped charging late fines on children's books. Over the next twelve months, the share of children's books returned within two weeks of the due date rose from 81 percent to 88 percent, and the number of new children's library cards rose by 12 percent. The library still charged fines on adult books, and that fine revenue stayed about the same. This month, the library board voted to end late fines on adult books as well, starting in January.

Which predictions are supported by the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Fine revenue from adult books will most likely drop after January.
Children's books will soon fall back to an 81 percent return rate.
Timely returns of adult books may improve after January, as they did for children's books.
The library will probably cut staff hours next year to make up for the lost fine revenue.
Adult books will most likely be returned late more often once their fines end.
R.w: Ending fines on children's books was followed by better returns, so a similar change for adult books may have a similar result. And once adult fines end, the adult fine revenue the library has been collecting will fall.

n.1: Nothing suggests the children's policy will change, so a reversal of the trend has no stated cause.
n.3: Staff cuts require an unstated event; the passage never mentions budgets or staffing.
n.4: The only evidence, from children's books, shows timely returns rising after fines ended; nothing points to more late returns.

R.q:
After her first two evening shifts at the new urgent care center, Brianna told her roommate, "Both nights, the waiting room was nearly empty by 9 p.m. People in this town obviously don't use urgent care in the evening. The center should close at 8 and save money on staff." The center had opened the week before, during a holiday, when many families were out of town.

Which fallacy does Brianna's reasoning contain?
o: Appeal to tradition
Post hoc
Circular reasoning
Hasty generalization
R.w: Brianna draws a broad conclusion about the whole town's habits from two nights, and those nights fell during an unusual holiday week. That is a hasty generalization from too few, unrepresentative examples.

n.0: She makes no appeal to how things have always been done; the center is brand new.
n.1: Brianna does not claim that one event caused a later one; she generalizes from a small sample.
n.2: Her conclusion rests on observations, not on a restatement of itself; the problem is the tiny sample.

M.q: Solve for x: (x + 3)/5 = (x - 1)/3.
M.w: Cross-multiply: 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1). Distribute: 3x + 9 = 5x - 5. Subtract 3x and add 5: 14 = 2x, so x = 7. Check: 10/5 = 2 and 6/3 = 2.

n.0: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 3x + 3 = 5x - 1 instead of 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1).
n.2: Sign error in the last step: -2x = -14 gives a positive x.
n.3: This distributes on the left but not on the right: 3x + 9 = 5x - 1.

M.q: During one shift, a patient drinks 2 cups of broth, 6 fluid ounces of juice, and 3 tablespoons of a liquid supplement. Use 1 cup = 240 milliliters and 1 fluid ounce = 30 milliliters. What is the patient's total intake? Enter the number of milliliters.

tr.675: Used 5 mL (a teaspoon) for each tablespoon.
tr.750: Counted each tablespoon as 1 fluid ounce (30 mL); 1 tbsp = 15 mL.

M.w: Broth: 2 × 240 = 480 mL. Juice: 6 × 30 = 180 mL. Supplement: 3 × 15 = 45 mL. Total = 480 + 180 + 45 = 705 mL.

M.q: Two bar graphs are placed side by side. Hospital X's graph has a vertical axis from 0 to 50 and shows 40 infections. Hospital Y's graph has a vertical axis from 0 to 500 and shows 400 infections. Both bars reach 80% of the way up their axes. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Hospital Y had 10 times as many infections as Hospital X
The hospitals had about the same number of infections
Hospital X had 10 times as many infections as Hospital Y
Hospital Y had 80% more infections than Hospital X
M.w: Read each bar against its own scale: X = 40 and Y = 400. 400 / 40 = 10, so Y had 10 times as many, even though the bars look equal.

n.1: The bars look equal only because the two graphs use different scales.
n.2: This reverses the comparison; Y's value, 400, is the larger one.
n.3: 80% is how far each bar reaches up its own axis, not a comparison between the hospitals.

M.q: A clinic uses the formula B = 703w / h² to calculate body mass index, where w is weight in pounds and h is height in inches. Which equation gives w in terms of B and h?
o: w = 703Bh²
w = Bh²/703
w = 703B/h²
M.w: Multiply both sides by h²: Bh² = 703w. Divide both sides by 703: w = Bh²/703.

n.0: This multiplies by 703 instead of dividing. 703 multiplies w in the formula, so dividing by 703 undoes it.
n.1: This divides by h² instead of multiplying. h² is a divisor in the formula, so multiplying by h² undoes it.
n.3: This leaves 703 in the numerator and h² in the denominator. To isolate w, multiply both sides by h² and divide both sides by 703.

M.q: A uniform store records the sizes of the last 10 pairs of nursing clogs it sold: 8, 9, 7.5, 9, 10, 8, 9, 11, 8.5, 9. What is the mode of the sizes sold?
M.w: The mode is the value that occurs most often. Size 9 appears 4 times, more than any other size.

n.0: 89 / 10 = 8.9 is the mean of the sizes.
n.1: Size 8 appears only twice, fewer times than size 9.
n.3: 4 is how many times size 9 appears, not the size itself.

M.q: Three patients are in consecutive even-numbered rooms. The sum of the three room numbers is 642. What is the lowest of the three room numbers?
M.w: Let the rooms be n, n + 2, and n + 4. Then 3n + 6 = 642, so 3n = 636 and n = 212. Check: 212 + 214 + 216 = 642.

n.0: This is the middle room number (642 ÷ 3), not the lowest.
n.1: This is the highest of the three room numbers.
n.2: This uses consecutive integers (n, n + 1, n + 2), giving 3n + 3 = 642. Consecutive even numbers differ by 2.

M.q: A researcher graphs how the dose of a pain reliever, in milligrams, affects the time until a patient reports relief, in minutes. How should the axes of the graph be labeled?
o: Dose on the y-axis, because the dose is what the researcher controls
Time until relief on the x-axis, because time is the independent variable
Either variable on either axis, since the graph shows a correlation
Dose on the x-axis and time until relief on the y-axis
M.w: The independent variable (dose, which the researcher sets) goes on the x-axis, and the dependent variable (time until relief, which responds) goes on the y-axis.

n.0: The variable the researcher controls is independent and belongs on the x-axis, not the y-axis.
n.1: Time is often independent, but here the time until relief is the response to the dose, so it is dependent.
n.2: Convention places the independent variable on the x-axis so the graph shows how y responds to x.

M.q: A clinic's goal is for each team to complete more than 0.7 of its training modules. Which of the following completion values are greater than 0.7? Select all that apply.

n.2: 9/13 ≈ 0.692, which is less than 0.7.
n.5: 7/10 = 0.7 exactly; it is equal to 0.7, not greater than it.

M.q: A square patio has an area of 90 square feet, so each side is √90 feet long. Between which two consecutive whole numbers does √90 lie?
o: 45 and 46
8 and 9
9 and 10
10 and 11
M.w: 9² = 81 and 10² = 100. Since 81 < 90 < 100, √90 is between 9 and 10 (about 9.49).

n.0: 45 is 90 ÷ 2; taking a square root is not the same as halving the number.
n.1: 9² = 81, which is already less than 90, so √90 is greater than 9.
n.3: 10² = 100, which is already greater than 90, so √90 is less than 10.

M.q: The mean of 8 blood glucose readings is 115 mg/dL. When one reading is removed, the mean of the remaining 7 readings is 110 mg/dL. What was the value of the removed reading, in mg/dL?

tr.120: 115 + 5, adding the change in the mean
tr.112.5: the average of the two means

M.w: Total of 8 readings = 8 x 115 = 920. Total of 7 readings = 7 x 110 = 770. Removed reading = 920 - 770 = 150 mg/dL.

M.q: Five containers are being compared for a supply room. Use 3.14 for pi and 1 milliliter = 1 cubic centimeter. Place the containers in order from least volume to greatest volume, starting with the least.
o: A bottle that holds 0.95 L
A cube with 10 cm edges
A jug that holds 1,020 mL
A box 8 cm by 12 cm by 11 cm
A cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 12 cm
M.w: Convert each to cubic centimeters: cylinder = 3.14 × 5² × 12 = 942; bottle = 0.95 L = 950 mL = 950; cube = 10³ = 1,000; jug = 1,020; box = 8 × 12 × 11 = 1,056. Least to greatest: 942, 950, 1,000, 1,020, 1,056.

M.q: The daily patient census on a medical unit for one week was 28, 31, 24, 35, 29, 22, and 33. What is the range of the daily census for the week?
M.w: Range = maximum - minimum = 35 - 22 = 13.

n.0: 33 - 28 = 5 subtracts the first value from the last as listed, not the minimum from the maximum.
n.2: 35 - 24 = 11 uses 24 as the minimum, but 22 is smaller.
n.3: 31 - 22 = 9 uses 31 as the maximum, but 35 is larger.

M.q: The mean of six lab values is 40. A seventh lab value of 61 is added to the data set. What is the mean of all seven values?
M.w: Original total = 6 x 40 = 240. New total = 240 + 61 = 301. New mean = 301 / 7 = 43.

n.0: 301 / 6 = 50.2 divides the new total by the old count.
n.2: 40 + 21 / 6 = 43.5 spreads the extra 21 over 6 values instead of 7.
n.3: (40 + 61) / 2 = 50.5 averages the old mean with the new value as if they had equal weight.

M.q: A patient-education poster is enlarged proportionally from a draft that is 8 inches wide and 10 inches tall. The poster is 26 inches wide. How tall is the poster? Enter the number of inches.

tr.28: Added the 18-inch increase in width to the height instead of scaling.
tr.20.8: Set up the ratio upside down (26 × 8 ÷ 10).

M.w: Set up width/height: 8/10 = 26/h. Cross-multiply: 8h = 260, so h = 32.5 inches.

M.q: A gazebo floor is shaped like a regular hexagon. A carpenter needs the angle at each corner to cut the floorboards. What is the measure of each interior angle of the floor?
M.w: Sum of interior angles = (n - 2) × 180 = (6 - 2) × 180 = 720°. Each angle = 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.

n.1: 108° is each interior angle of a regular pentagon (5 sides).
n.2: 720° is the sum of all six interior angles; divide by 6.
n.3: 60° is each exterior angle (360 ÷ 6); an interior angle and its exterior angle sum to 180°.

M.q: Mia earns $18.40 per hour for her first 40 hours each week and 1.5 times that rate for every hour over 40. Last week she worked 46.5 hours. What was her total pay?

n.0: $1,283.40 pays all 46.5 hours at the overtime rate.
n.1: $855.60 pays all 46.5 hours at the regular rate.
n.2: $901.60 counts only 6 overtime hours instead of 6.5.

M.q: A nurse begins a 12.5-hour shift at 6:45 p.m. She stays 40 minutes after the shift ends to finish charting. At what time does she leave?
M.w: 12.5 hours = 12 hours 30 minutes. 6:45 p.m. + 12 hours = 6:45 a.m.; + 30 minutes = 7:15 a.m. (end of shift); + 40 minutes = 7:55 a.m.

n.1: This reads 12.5 hours as 12 hours 50 minutes; 0.5 hour is 30 minutes.
n.2: Twelve and a half hours after 6:45 p.m. is the next morning, so the time is a.m.
n.3: This is when the shift ends; the 40 minutes of charting must be added.

M.q: A health department wants to show the distribution of cholesterol levels for 200 adults, grouped into intervals of 20 mg/dL, so that readers can see where most levels fall. Which display is most appropriate?
o: Line graph
Circle graph
Scatterplot
Histogram
M.w: A histogram shows the distribution of one numeric variable grouped into intervals, with bar heights giving the frequency in each interval.

n.0: A line graph shows change over time, and these data have no time order.
n.1: A circle graph shows parts of a whole and makes the shape of a distribution hard to see.
n.2: A scatterplot needs two numeric variables, but only cholesterol level is given.

M.q: A research lab recorded five room temperatures, some in degrees Celsius and some in degrees Fahrenheit. Place the readings in order from coldest to warmest, starting with the coldest.
M.w: Convert the Celsius readings to °F with °F = (9/5)(°C) + 32: 14 °C = 57.2 °F; 15 °C = 59 °F; 16.5 °C = 61.7 °F. Coldest to warmest: 57.2 °F (14 °C), 58 °F, 59 °F (15 °C), 61 °F, 61.7 °F (16.5 °C).

M.q: A 1,000 mL IV bag starts infusing at 0800 at 125 mL per hour. At 1130 the rate is reduced to 75 mL per hour. Assuming the infusion continues without stopping, how many milliliters remain in the bag at 1400? Enter the number of milliliters only.

tr.250: Used 125 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.550: Used 75 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.625: Gave the volume infused instead of the volume remaining.

M.q: It takes 6 nurses 8 hours to complete a set of patient assessments. Working at the same rate, how many hours would it take 4 nurses to complete the same set of assessments?
o: 10 hours
12 hours
About 5.3 hours
6 hours
M.w: Fewer workers need more time: an inverse relationship with a constant product. 6 x 8 = 48 nurse-hours. 48 / 4 = 12 hours.

n.0: Adding 1 hour per missing nurse is not supported; the total work, 48 nurse-hours, must be shared.
n.2: 8 x 4 / 6 = 5.3 treats the relationship as direct, as if fewer nurses would finish sooner.
n.3: Fewer nurses cannot finish sooner; subtracting 2 hours reverses the relationship.

M.q: A travel nurse worked 38.5, 41.2, 39.8, 40.6 and 39.1 hours over five weeks. Which is the best estimate of the total number of hours she worked?
M.w: All five values cluster near 40, so estimate 5 × 40 = 200 hours. (Exact: 199.2 hours.)

n.0: 40 is the typical hours in one week, not the total for all five weeks.
n.2: 220 rounds every value up to the next ten (40 + 50 + 40 + 50 + 40) instead of to the nearest ten.
n.3: 170 truncates each value to the tens place (30 + 40 + 30 + 40 + 30) instead of rounding.

M.q: A board is 8 feet 3 inches long. A carpenter cuts off a piece that is 2 feet 7 inches long. Ignoring the width of the saw cut, how long is the remaining piece of board?
o: 5 ft 8 in
6 ft 8 in
5 ft 6 in
6 ft 4 in
M.w: Borrow 1 foot: 8 ft 3 in = 7 ft 15 in. 7 ft 15 in - 2 ft 7 in = 5 ft 8 in. Check: 99 in - 31 in = 68 in = 5 ft 8 in.

n.1: This borrows 12 inches correctly but does not reduce the 8 feet to 7 feet.
n.2: This borrows 1 foot as 10 inches (13 - 7 = 6); 1 ft = 12 in, so 15 - 7 = 8.
n.3: This subtracts 3 from 7 instead of borrowing a foot from the 8 feet.

M.q: A decorative window is shaped like a semicircle with a straight bottom edge 4 feet long. A builder needs trim for the entire edge of the window, including the curved part and the straight bottom. How many feet of trim are needed? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: Curved part = 1/2 × πd = 1/2 × 3.14 × 4 = 6.28 ft. Add the straight edge (the diameter): 6.28 + 4 = 10.28 ft.

n.0: This adds the 4-foot straight edge to a full circle's circumference instead of half of it.
n.1: This is the circumference of a full circle (3.14 × 4).
n.3: This is the curved part by itself; the 4-foot straight edge must be added.

M.q: A patient gained 4.15 pounds between two weekly weigh-ins. Which mixed number, in lowest terms, is equal to 4.15?
M.w: The decimal part has two places: 0.15 = 15/100. Divide both terms by 5: 3/20. So 4.15 = 4 3/20.

n.0: 4 1/15 treats the digits after the decimal point as a denominator (4.0666...).
n.1: 4 3/10 = 4.3. It divides 15 by 5 but 100 by 10.
n.2: 4 3/200 = 4.015. It uses 1,000 as the denominator instead of 100.

M.q: Four patients' meal trays were checked after lunch. Ana ate 5/8 of her meal, Ben ate 0.63 of his, Carmen ate 61% of hers and Dev ate 3/5 of his. Who ate the greatest portion?
o: Ana
Carmen
Dev
Ben
M.w: Convert to decimals: Ana 5/8 = 0.625, Ben 0.63 = 0.630, Carmen 61% = 0.61, Dev 3/5 = 0.6. The greatest is 0.630, so Ben ate the most.

n.0: 5/8 = 0.625, which is slightly less than 0.630.
n.1: 61% = 0.61, which is less than 0.625 and 0.63.
n.2: 3/5 = 0.6, the least of the four portions.

M.q: Plan A for a cell phone costs $20 per month plus $0.08 per minute. Plan B costs a flat $35 per month. Which inequality gives the numbers of minutes m for which Plan A costs less than Plan B?
M.w: Plan A < Plan B: 20 + 0.08m < 35. Subtract 20: 0.08m < 15. Divide by 0.08: m < 187.5.

n.0: This divides $35 by $0.08 without first subtracting Plan A's $20 monthly charge.
n.2: This divides Plan A's $20 monthly charge by $0.08 instead of the $15 difference.
n.3: This reverses the direction. Plan A's cost grows with every minute, so it is cheaper for fewer minutes, not more.

M.q: Solve the proportion (x + 2)/9 = 4/6.
M.w: Cross-multiply: 6(x + 2) = 4 × 9 = 36. Divide by 6: x + 2 = 6. Subtract 2: x = 4. Check: 6/9 = 2/3 and 4/6 = 2/3.

n.0: This flips the second ratio, solving (x + 2)/9 = 6/4.
n.1: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 6x + 2 = 36 instead of 6(x + 2) = 36.
n.2: This uses addition: 9 is 3 more than 6, so it adds 3 to 4. Proportions scale by multiplying.

M.q: A clinic is buying hand sanitizer. Select the price of the bottle size with the lowest cost per fluid ounce.

n.a: $3.12 is the lowest total price, but 3.12 / 8 = $0.39 per fl oz, tied for the highest unit price.
n.b: 4.44 / 12 = $0.37 per fl oz, which is more than $0.36.
n.c: 6.24 / 16 = $0.39 per fl oz, tied for the highest unit price.
n.e: 11.84 / 32 = $0.37 per fl oz, which is more than $0.36.
n.f: The largest bottle is often assumed to be the best buy, but 23.68 / 64 = $0.37 per fl oz, which is more than $0.36.

M.q: Pharmacy A fills 135 prescriptions in 9 hours. Pharmacy B fills 48 prescriptions in 2 hours 40 minutes. How many more prescriptions per hour does Pharmacy B fill than Pharmacy A?
M.w: Pharmacy A: 135 ÷ 9 = 15 per hour. Pharmacy B: 2 hours 40 minutes = 2 2/3 hours = 160 minutes; 48 ÷ 160 = 0.3 per minute × 60 = 18 per hour. Difference: 18 - 15 = 3.

n.1: This reads 2 hours 40 minutes as 2.4 hours, giving 48 ÷ 2.4 = 20 per hour for Pharmacy B.
n.2: This is Pharmacy B's rate, not the difference between the two rates.
n.3: This is Pharmacy A's rate, not the difference between the two rates.

M.q: A multidose vial contains 20 mL of medication, and 4.5 mL has already been drawn from it. Each dose is 1.5 mL. How many more full doses can be drawn from the vial?
M.w: Medication left: 20 - 4.5 = 15.5 mL. Doses: 15.5 ÷ 1.5 = 10.33. Only complete doses count, so round down: 10 full doses (10 × 1.5 = 15 mL; 0.5 mL is left over).

n.1: 14 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn and also rounds 13.33 up instead of down.
n.2: 11 rounds 10.33 up; 11 doses would need 16.5 mL, but only 15.5 mL is left.
n.3: 13 ignores the 4.5 mL already drawn (20 ÷ 1.5 = 13.33, rounded down).

M.q: A study of 30 hospitals found a strong positive correlation between the number of parking spaces and the number of patient falls reported each year. Which conclusion is best supported by this finding?
o: Reducing parking spaces will reduce patient falls
The link is a coincidence, since parking cannot affect falls
Adding parking spaces will lead to more patient falls
Both may rise with a third factor, such as hospital size
M.w: Correlation does not show causation. Larger hospitals have more parking and more patients, so more falls are reported; a third variable can explain both.

n.0: This also assumes cause and effect, just in the other direction of change.
n.1: A strong correlation across 30 hospitals is a real pattern, not chance; a third variable such as hospital size explains it.
n.2: This claims parking causes falls; a correlation alone does not show cause and effect.

M.q: A trend line was fit to data on daily water intake and age for a sample of adults aged 20 to 60. For which age is a prediction made from the trend line least reliable?
o: 41 years
85 years
25 years
58 years
M.w: Predicting within the range of the data (interpolation) is reasonable. Age 85 is far outside the 20 to 60 range, so that prediction is an extrapolation and the least reliable.

n.0: 41 is near the middle of the data, where the trend line is best supported.
n.2: 25 is inside the 20 to 60 range, so it is an interpolation.
n.3: 58 is near the upper end but still inside the 20 to 60 range of the data.

M.q: A table summarizes a screening test given to 500 people. Tested positive and have the condition: 45. Tested positive and do not have the condition: 15. Tested negative and have the condition: 5. Tested negative and do not have the condition: 435. Of the people who tested positive, what percent actually have the condition? Enter the number only.

tr.12: the percent of all 500 people who tested positive
tr.90: 45 out of the 50 people who have the condition

M.w: 'Of the people who tested positive' sets the denominator: 45 + 15 = 60. Of these, 45 have the condition. 45 / 60 = 0.75 = 75%.

M.q: A triangular flower bed has sides of 13 meters, 14 meters, and 15 meters. The perpendicular height from the 14-meter side to the opposite corner is 12 meters. What is the area of the flower bed?
o: 42 m²
84 m²
168 m²
105 m²
M.w: A = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × 14 × 12 = 84 m². The 13 m and 15 m sides are slanted, so they are not the height.

n.0: 42 m is the perimeter (13 + 14 + 15), not the area.
n.2: This multiplies base by height but leaves out the 1/2.
n.3: This uses the 15 m slanted side as the height (1/2 × 14 × 15); the height must be perpendicular to the base.

M.q: A medical assistant's hourly wage rose from $18.40 to $20.70. What was the percent increase in the hourly wage? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.11.11: Divided the $2.30 raise by the new wage, $20.70, instead of the original wage.
tr.2.3: Reported the dollar increase instead of the percent increase.

M.q: A lab technician records a reagent concentration as 0.045. Which list contains three values that are each equivalent to 0.045?
M.w: 0.045 × 100 = 4.5%. As a fraction, 0.045 has three decimal places: 45/1,000. Dividing both terms by 5 gives 9/200. All three values in that list equal 0.045.

n.1: Every value in this list equals 0.45, ten times 0.045.
n.2: 4.5% and 45/1,000 are correct, but 9/20 = 0.45, so the list fails.
n.3: Every value in this list equals 0.0045, one tenth of 0.045.

M.q: A clinic gave 640 flu shots in October and 512 flu shots in November. What was the percent decrease in flu shots from October to November?
M.w: Change = 640 - 512 = 128. Percent change = 128 ÷ 640 × 100 = 20% decrease.

n.1: This is November's total as a percent of October's, not the percent decrease.
n.2: This divides the change by the new value, 512. Percent change divides by the original value, 640.
n.3: This turns the 128-shot drop into a percent without dividing it by the original value.

S.q: A student grows bean plants with 0, 5, 10 or 15 g of fertilizer per pot, using the same soil, pot size and daily water. After three weeks she measures each plant's height. What is the dependent variable?
o: Plant height after three weeks
Type of soil used in each pot
Mass of fertilizer in each pot
Volume of water given each day
S.w: The dependent variable is what is measured in response to the change; here, plant height. The fertilizer mass is what she deliberately changes (independent variable).
